angle: angle 1 · a place and a time
title: Main Street, 1957: A Walk Through the Town We Lost

scenes.text: It's a Saturday morning in nineteen fifty-seven, and you're standing at the corner of Main Street. The sun is shining on the brick buildings. Cars are parked at an angle along the curb. A bell rings over a shop door. Somebody waves at you from across the street, because in this town, everybody knows everybody.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY, 1957

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-seven, almost every town in America had a street like this. It might have been called Main Street, Front Street, Broadway or Market Street. But it was always the heart of the town. It was where you shopped, ate, banked, got your hair cut, saw a movie and caught up on all the news.
scenes.caption: THE HEART OF THE TOWN

scenes.text: So let's take a walk. Door by door, block by block, down a typical American Main Street in nineteen fifty-seven. If you grew up in a small town, I think you'll recognize every single place we stop.
scenes.caption: LET'S TAKE A WALK

scenes.text: Our first stop is the corner drugstore. Through the glass door, you can smell it before you see it. Medicine, perfume, coffee and fresh-made grilled cheese. On one side, the pharmacist works behind a high counter. On the other side, there's the soda fountain, with a long marble counter and a row of red stools.
scenes.caption: THE CORNER DRUGSTORE

scenes.text: The soda jerk wears a white paper hat. He makes a cherry Coke by pumping syrup into a glass and adding carbonated water. A chocolate malted costs about twenty-five cents. A banana split, maybe thirty-five. Teenagers crowd the booths after school, and old men drink coffee at the counter every morning.
scenes.caption: THE SODA JERK

scenes.text: The pharmacist knows everyone in town by name. He knows who has a bad heart and whose baby has a cough. If you call late at night with a sick child, he might open the store just for you. There's a rack of comic books near the door, and a magazine stand with Life, Look and The Saturday Evening Post.
scenes.caption: HE KNOWS YOUR NAME

scenes.text: Next door is the five-and-dime. Woolworth's, Kresge's, Ben Franklin, or a local store just like them. Wooden floors that creak when you walk. Long counters piled with everything you could need. Thread, buttons, yarn, sewing patterns, kitchen gadgets, school supplies, cheap toys, goldfish and parakeets.
scenes.query: 1950s five and dime store interior counters
scenes.caption: THE FIVE-AND-DIME

scenes.text: Kids love the five-and-dime, because it's the one store where their allowance goes a long way. A quarter can buy a bag of candy, a balsa wood airplane, or a little plastic toy. Many of those stores also have a lunch counter, where shoppers stop for a grilled cheese, a slice of pie and a cup of coffee.
scenes.caption: WHERE A QUARTER GOES FAR

scenes.text: Across the street is the hardware store, and it's a world of its own. The smell of oil, rope and fresh-cut keys. Nails sold by the pound from wooden bins. Paint mixed by hand. Garden seeds in paper packets. Every tool a man could want, hanging on pegboard walls.
scenes.caption: THE HARDWARE STORE

scenes.text: The owner can tell you exactly what you need, even if you can only describe it. You bring in the broken part, and he finds you a match. He'll explain how to fix a leaky faucet or sharpen a lawnmower blade. And if you're a little short on cash this week, he'll put it on your account.
scenes.caption: PUT IT ON MY ACCOUNT

scenes.text: In the middle of the block is the biggest building on Main Street. The department store. In a bigger town, it might be a J.C. Penney, a Sears or a local family store with the founder's name painted on the side. Inside, there are glass display cases, high ceilings and an elevator with an operator who calls out each floor.
scenes.caption: THE DEPARTMENT STORE

scenes.text: Women shop for dresses, hats, gloves and stockings. Men buy suits, shirts and neckties. Children get measured for new school shoes, and some stores have a machine called a shoe-fitting fluoroscope, which uses X-rays so you can see your toes wiggling inside the shoes. It sounds incredible today, but kids loved it.
scenes.caption: THE X-RAY SHOE MACHINE

scenes.text: When you pay, the clerk might put your money in a little container and send it zooming along a wire or through a pneumatic tube to the cashier upstairs. A moment later, your change comes zooming back. At Christmastime, the store windows are filled with displays, and Santa sits in a big chair on the toy floor.
scenes.caption: CHANGE BY TUBE

scenes.text: Down the street is the barbershop, with its spinning red, white and blue pole. Inside, there are two or three big leather chairs, a row of waiting chairs, and a stack of old magazines. A haircut costs around a dollar. The radio plays a ballgame, and the men argue about politics and fishing.
scenes.caption: THE BARBERSHOP
scenes.chapter: The barbershop and the beauty shop

scenes.text: Little boys get a crew cut or a flattop, sitting on a board laid across the arms of the chair. The barber finishes with a splash of tonic and a dusting of powder on the neck. And for the grown men, there's a hot towel shave with a straight razor, and maybe a shoeshine on the way out.
scenes.caption: A FLATTOP

scenes.text: A few doors away is the beauty shop, where the women of the town get their hair washed and set. They sit under big hooded dryers, reading magazines and catching up on every bit of news in town. Many people say the beauty shop was the real newspaper of a small town. If it happened, they knew about it there.
scenes.caption: THE REAL NEWSPAPER

scenes.text: On the corner stands the bank, built of stone, with tall columns and a big clock out front. Inside, the floors are marble, and the tellers sit behind brass cages. Children bring in their piggy banks to open a passbook savings account. And the bank president knows every farmer and business owner in the county.
scenes.caption: THE BANK
scenes.chapter: The bank, the post office and the newspaper

scenes.text: Across the street is the post office, with the American flag flying out front. Inside, there's a wall of little brass mailboxes with tiny glass windows. A stamp costs three cents. Wanted posters hang on the bulletin board. And the postmaster, who's held the job for twenty years, knows everyone's handwriting.
scenes.caption: 3-CENT STAMP

scenes.text: And there's the newspaper office, with the presses rumbling in the back. The weekly paper reports everything. Who's visiting from out of town. Whose cow won at the county fair. Births, weddings, deaths, and the high school football scores. In a town like this, getting your name in the paper is a very big deal.
scenes.caption: YOUR NAME IN THE PAPER

scenes.text: By now, you're hungry. So let's stop at the diner. It might be a shiny steel railroad car diner, or a little café with a counter and a few booths. The cook works the grill where everyone can see him. The waitress calls you honey and refills your coffee before you ask.
scenes.caption: THE DINER

scenes.text: A hamburger costs about thirty cents. A plate of meatloaf with mashed potatoes and green beans is around seventy-five cents. And there's always pie. Apple, cherry, coconut cream, lemon meringue. Every table has a little jukebox selector, where a nickel buys you one song.
scenes.caption: PIE

scenes.text: The diner is where the town really talks. Farmers come in early, before sunrise. Businessmen come for lunch. Teenagers come after the movie. Police officers stop by on their rounds. Everybody's welcome, and almost everybody stops in sooner or later.
scenes.caption: EVERYBODY'S WELCOME

scenes.text: Halfway down the block, you can't miss it. The movie theater, with its big marquee full of light bulbs, and black letters announcing what's playing. In nineteen fifty-seven, that might be The Bridge on the River Kwai, An Affair to Remember, or Elvis Presley in Jailhouse Rock.
scenes.caption: THE MARQUEE

scenes.text: On Saturday afternoon, it's the kids' matinee. For a quarter, children get cartoons, a newsreel, a cowboy serial and a full feature. They throw popcorn, shout at the screen, and cheer for the hero. Parents drop them off at noon and pick them up at four, and everybody's happy.
scenes.caption: THE SATURDAY MATINEE

scenes.text: Inside, the theater is grand, with velvet curtains, a balcony, and painted ceilings. An usher in a uniform shows you to your seat with a flashlight. Popcorn costs a dime. For many small towns, the theater is the most beautiful building in town, and the place where first dates and first kisses happen.
scenes.caption: THE MOST BEAUTIFUL BUILDING

scenes.text: As the sun goes down, Main Street fills up. Saturday night is the big night of the week. Farm families come into town to shop, visit and see a movie. Stores stay open late. People stroll up and down the sidewalk, stopping to talk with friends and neighbors they haven't seen all week.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY NIGHT

scenes.text: Teenagers cruise the street in their cars, around and around, radios playing. Old men sit on a bench outside the hardware store, watching the world go by. Kids beg for one more ice cream cone. In many towns, there's a band concert in the park, or a dance at the American Legion hall.
scenes.caption: AROUND AND AROUND

scenes.text: So what happened to that Main Street? In the years after nineteen fifty-seven, America changed in ways that slowly emptied it. The interstate highways, which started in nineteen fifty-six, made it easy to drive past small towns, or to drive out to a bigger one.
scenes.caption: THE INTERSTATE

scenes.text: Shopping centers and malls grew up on the edge of town, with free parking and everything under one roof. The first fully enclosed mall in America, Southdale Center in Minnesota, had opened just a year earlier, in nineteen fifty-six. Over the next thirty years, thousands of malls followed.
scenes.caption: SOUTHDALE, 1956

scenes.text: Then came the big discount stores. Kmart in nineteen sixty-two. Walmart, the same year. They offered lower prices than any small shop could match. One by one, the drugstore, the hardware store, the five-and-dime and the department store closed. In many towns, the movie theater went dark too.
scenes.caption: 1962: KMART AND WALMART

scenes.text: By the nineteen eighties, many Main Streets were half empty. Boarded-up windows. For Lease signs. The bank building turned into a law office, or nothing at all. In nineteen eighty, the National Trust for Historic Preservation started the Main Street program, to try to bring those downtowns back to life.
scenes.caption: FOR LEASE

scenes.text: Some of them have come back. Today, many small towns have restored their old Main Streets, with coffee shops, bakeries and antique stores in the old buildings. But something is different. The pharmacist who knew your name, the barber who'd cut your hair since you were three, and the Saturday nights when the whole town came out are mostly memories now.
scenes.query: small town main street brick buildings
scenes.caption: SOME HAVE COME BACK

scenes.text: What we lost wasn't just stores. It was a way of living. A place where you couldn't walk a block without saying hello to someone. Where business was done on a handshake. Where you were part of a town, not just a customer. For many people, that's what they miss the most.
scenes.caption: A WAY OF LIVING

scenes.text: If you grew up on a Main Street like this, you carry it with you. The bell over the door. The squeak of the stool at the soda fountain. The light of the marquee. The smell of the hardware store. It's still there, every time you close your eyes.
scenes.caption: THE BELL OVER THE DOOR

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was the name of your town, and what was the name of its Main Street? What store do you miss the most? We read every comment. Next, we're looking at what it was like to become a mother in nineteen fifty-five. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR TOWN?
